title: Bloodstream Infections After Cardiac Surgery: Pathogen Distribution, Antimicrobial Resistance, and a Nomogram Prediction Model
authors: Shuxian Miao; Yanfei Lu; Jue Wang; Wei Zhang; Wenying Xia; Yuqiao Xu
abstract: Background: Postoperative bloodstream infection (BSI) is a severe complication following cardiac surgery, associated with significant mortality. This study aims to characterize pathogen profiles, antimicrobial resistance and independent risk factors for BSI in a Chinese cardiac surgery cohort. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of postoperative BSI in patients who underwent cardiac surgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University from January 2019 to December 2024. Patients who developed postoperative BSI were identified and a 1:1 propensity score matched analysis were performed to adjust for baseline characteristics of patients. Univariate and multivariate analysis were applied to identify independent risk factors for postoperative BSI. R software was used to construct a prediction nomogram, followed by internal validation. Results: During the study, a total of 10,007 patients underwent heart surgery, and 164 pairs of patients were successfully matched using propensity score matching. Gram-negative bacteria were the most common pathogens (64.1%), followed by Fungi (18.2%) and Gram-positive bacteria (17.6%). Among Enterobacterales , 33.8% were carbapenem-resistant, with carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) accounting for 63.6% of K. pneumoniae isolates. Meanwhile, 85.0% (17/20) of A. baumannii isolates were multidrug-resistant A. baumannii (MDRAB). The 90-day mortality rate in the BSI group was 39.0%, significantly higher than that in the non-BSI group (4.9%, P < 0.001). Multivariate logistic regression identified impaired cardiac function (New York Heart Association II–IV, NYHA II–IV) (OR=5.583, 95% CI:2.681– 11.627), pulmonary infection (OR =4.053, 95% CI:1.692– 9.710), emergency surgery (OR=9.629, 95% CI:2.962– 31.301), coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) (OR=2.796, 95% CI:1.096– 7.134), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT Postoperative ICU stay ≥ 14 d) (OR=4.758, 95% CI:1.854– 12.211) and postoperative ICU stay ≥ 14 d (OR=14.616, 95% CI:6.765– 31.577) as independent risk factors for postoperative BSI. The nomogram showed good discrimination and calibration after internal validation, with an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.913 and a mean absolute calibration error of 0.026. Conclusion: Postoperative BSI in cardiac surgery patients is associated with high mortality. A nomogram based on impaired cardiac function (NYHA II–IV), pulmonary infection, emergency surgery, CABG, CRRT and postoperative ICU stay ≥ 14 d displayed high accuracy and consistency in predicting the risk of postoperative BSI. These results facilitate early risk stratification and guide preventive strategies in high-risk cardiac surgical patients. Keywords: cardiac surgery, bloodstream infection, multi-resistant bacteria, risk factors, coronary artery bypass grafting, nomogram prediction model

title: Association of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy with cardiovascular outcomes in patients with MASLD: A translational study
authors: Chun-Chi Yang; Jheng-Yan Wu; Yu‐Min Ko; Shu-Chi Wang; Ya‐Yun Cheng; Ming-Lung Yu; Wei‐Ting Chang
abstract: Patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) are at increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes, potentially involving systemic metabolic dysfunction and cardiac remodeling. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve metabolic dysfunction in MASLD; however, their associations with cardiovascular outcomes and effects on MASLD-associated cardiac remodeling remain incompletely understood. In this translational study, we integrated a real-world TriNetX cohort of patients with MASLD and T2D with complementary experimental studies in a mouse model of MASLD. Following propensity score matching, 42,910 patients were included in each treatment group. GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with a lower risk of the primary composite cardiovascular outcome compared with sulfonylurea therapy (hazard ratio 0.87, 95% confidence interval 0.84-0.91; P < 0.001), although this association was not statistically significant in 90-day and 180-day landmark analyses. In Western diet-fed mice, GLP-1 RA treatment improved selected indices of cardiac function and attenuated cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. Although myocardial fibrosis was numerically reduced, the difference compared with vehicle-treated mice was not statistically significant (P = 0.28). Molecular analyses showed reduced expression of fibrosis- and extracellular matrix remodeling-related markers, including CTGF, TGF-β1, and vimentin. Collectively, GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with lower cardiovascular risk in the primary observational analysis, although this finding was not consistently supported by sensitivity analyses. Complementary experimental findings suggest improvements in selected cardiac functional indices and changes in fibrosis-associated molecular remodeling, warranting further investigation.

title: Conventional risk factors and angiographic profile of young patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction in comparison with older patients
authors: Munna Rani Deb; M. Mukhlesur Rahman; Nusrat Jahan; Taslima Afroz; Farah Naz Huq; M. Najim Uddin; Gulam Mostafa
journal: International Journal of Research in Medical Sciences
abstract: Background: Globally, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of death and have a substantial influence on public health. It has been shown that ischemic heart disease accounts for a larger proportion of deaths among South Asians. Risk factors and angiographic profile differ significantly in young people compared to older patients. The aim of this study was to compare conventional risk factors and angiographic profile between young and older patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. Methods: This comparative study was conducted at the Department of Cardiology, Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital, Sylhet, from October 2022 to February 2025. Results: Regarding risk factors for STEMI, Smoking was the most common and significant risk factor in group I patients compared to group II patients (80%vs 62.7%). Compared with group I, group II patients had a significantly higher prevalence of hypertension(28%vs14.7%) and diabetes mellitus (34.7%vs 20.0%). In this study, the mean gensini score of the group I patients were less (27.22±21.20) compared with group II (41.52±30.80). Majority of the patients in group I had significant single vessel disease compared to group II (30.7%vs10.7%) (p<0.05). Patient with group II had statistically significant triple vessel disease than group I (40%vs13.3%) (p<0.05). Conclusions: Smoking is an important risk factor for development of ST elevation myocardial infarction in young patients, compared to older patients, where diabetes and hypertension were more significant. Young patients mostly present with SVD compared to older patients where multivessel disease were significantly higher.

title: Pre-existing heart failure subtype and in-hospital mortality in liver transplantation: a nationwide analysis
authors: Nithila Sivakumar; Chanokporn Puchongmart; Camila Padovese; Mohammed Abujulaydah; Ben Thiravetyan; Valmiki Maharaj
journal: International Journal of Research in Medical Sciences
abstract: Background: Heart failure (HF) is increasingly encountered in liver transplant candidates, yet the influence of HF phenotype on perioperative outcomes remains unclear. We evaluated the association between pre-existing HF subtype and in-hospital mortality among liver transplant hospitalizations. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of the National Inpatient Sample, 2016-2022. Adult liver transplant hospitalizations were stratified into no HF, chronic diastolic HF, and chronic systolic HF (surrogates for HF with preserved and reduced ejection fraction, respectively). The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included acute kidney injury, acute HF, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, discharge disposition, length of stay, and hospital charges. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, and hospital characteristics. Results: Among 53,910 weighted hospitalizations, 98.1% had no HF, 1.5% had chronic diastolic HF, and 0.4% had chronic systolic HF. Patients with chronic diastolic HF were older with a greater comorbidity burden, including hypertension, diabetes, arrhythmias, and renal failure (all p<0.01). Unadjusted in-hospital mortality was higher in chronic diastolic HF (5.7%) and chronic systolic HF (7.0%) than in no HF (2.9%; p=0.03), as were acute kidney injury, cardiac arrest, length of stay, and charges. After adjustment, neither chronic diastolic HF (adjusted odds ratio 1.6, 95% confidence interval 0.7-3.4) nor chronic systolic HF (2.1, 0.7-6.7) was independently associated with mortality. Conclusions: Pre-existing HF is associated with worse unadjusted outcomes in liver transplant hospitalizations, but HF subtype is not independently associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment. Comorbidity burden, rather than HF phenotype, appears to drive mortality risk in this highly selected population.

title: Achieving Project Performance through Stakeholder Participation Practices: Empirical Evidence from Catheterisation Laboratory Projects at Selected Healthcare Facilities in Nairobi City County, Kenya
authors: Francis Sitati Muliro; Morrisson Mutuku
journal: East African Journal of Business and Economics
abstract: Catheterisation laboratory (cath lab) projects are central to the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular disease, yet their performance in achieving intended goals remains a concern in Kenya. This study examined how stakeholder participation in project identification, funding, monitoring and evaluation, and capacity building influences the performance of cath lab projects at three healthcare facilities in Nairobi City County: Kenyatta National Hospital, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, and Avenue Hospital. General Systems Theory and Stakeholder Theory guided this descriptive survey, which had a qualitative component. The target population was 340 top and middle-level managers, departmental employees, patients, and representatives of government agencies and employee unions. Using Taro Yamane's formula and proportionate stratified random sampling, 184 respondents were selected and 157 returned usable questionnaires (85.3%). Data were collected through a semi-structured questionnaire and interviews with 12 cath lab beneficiaries, and were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple linear regression, and thematic analysis. All four forms of participation correlated positively and significantly with project performance (r = 0.611 to 0.706, p < 0.001). The regression model was significant and explained 70.3% of the variance in performance (adjusted R2 = 0.696; F(4, 152) = 89.9, p < 0.001). Funding (β = 0.644, p < 0.001) and monitoring and evaluation (β = 0.185, p = 0.001) were significant individual predictors, whereas project identification and capacity building were not once the other variables were controlled for, despite their strong bivariate correlations with performance. Interviewees highlighted communication on costs and timing, waiting-area privacy, and digital booking. The study concludes that stakeholder participation, particularly in funding and monitoring and evaluation, enhances cath lab project performance. Hospital managers and policymakers should institutionalise stakeholder participation across the project lifecycle, and future studies should extend to other countries and longitudinal designs.

title: Human PSC-Derived Cardiac Cells for Heart Failure: From Cell Therapy to Engineered Tissue Patches
authors: P. Heinrich; Eleonore Baier; Karl‐Ludwig Laugwitz; Christine M Poch; Alessandra Moretti
journal: Current Treatment Options in Cardiovascular Medicine
abstract: Abstract Purpose of Review This comprehensive overview evaluates recent progress in human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte therapies to improve the outcome of heart failure patients, with emphasis on delivery routes, early clinical employment, and the barriers for sustained functional cardiac repair. Recent Findings Multiple complementary strategies for cardiac remuscularization are being pursued in parallel, including single cell suspension, multicellular spheroids, cardiomyocyte sheets, and engineered myocardial tissues. Early clinical translation has established feasibility across several platforms, while engineered heart muscle has provided the clearest evidence of persistent graft retention and structural myocardial augmentation. Cardiomyocyte sheets have reached conditional regulatory approval, and catheter-based spheroid delivery is entering clinical evaluation. However, arrhythmogenicity, immune rejection, incomplete maturation and manufacturing complexity remain major challenges on the path to the clinic. Summary Pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiac products are transitioning from experimental concepts to clinically tested therapies. Future progress will depend on identifying the optimal patient population, product format and delivery route, reducing the need for immunosuppression, and demonstrating meaningful improvements in patient hospitalization, quality of life, and survival.

title: Association of red cell distribution width and platelet distribution width with angiographic severity of coronary artery disease in patients with stable angina: a cross-sectional study
authors: Ahmed Hussein; Mohammed Aliraqi; Hashim Zaki
abstract: Objective: To assess the associations of red cell distribution width-standard deviation (RDW-SD) and platelet distribution width (PDW) with angiographic coronary artery disease (CAD) severity, using the Gensini score, in adults undergoing coronary angiography for stable angina. Methods: This single-centre cross-sectional study recruited 65 consecutive adults who underwent coronary angiography for stable angina at Mosul Cardiac Centre, Iraq, between January and August 2025. A Gensini score ≥32 defined severe CAD. Clinical and laboratory measurements, including RDW-SD and PDW, were compared by severity. Spearman correlation, logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed. Results: Severe CAD occurred in 29/65 patients (44.6%); 36 (55.4%) had mild-to-moderate disease. RDW-SD was higher in severe CAD (45.85 ± 6.36 fL) than in mild-to-moderate disease (42.41 ± 3.25 fL; p = 0.003). RDW-SD correlated with Gensini score (rs = 0.358; p = 0.003) and remained associated after adjustment (adjusted OR, 1.320 per unit; 95% CI, 1.055–1.651; p = 0.015). RDW-SD AUC was 0.710 (95% CI, 0.582–0.837). PDW did not differ (15.60 ± 1.50 vs 15.80 ± 1.30 fL; p = 0.452) and showed poor discrimination (AUC, 0.430). Severe CAD also had higher fasting glucose and white blood cell count. Conclusions: In this single-centre study of stable angina, RDW-SD was related to the severity of CAD as defined by Gensini but not PDW in this sample. The discrimination of RDW-SD was limited-to-moderate. The preliminary results of this study need to be confirmed in a larger population before use in the clinic.

title: Biological Age, Frailty and Cardiovascular Care: A Pakistan-Focused Editorial Comment
authors: Shahadat Hussain Ch.; Nauman Ali
abstract: Cognitive impairment, frailty, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) are often approached as separate clinical problems. However, the recent American College of Cardiology (ACC) Scientific Statement presents a more integrated perspective, emphasizing their convergence in older adults and their close relationship with biological aging [1]. This framework is particularly relevant to Pakistan, where cardiovascular services increasingly encounter older patients with multimorbidity, delayed presentation, limited access to rehabilitation, and reduced functional reserve. The central message is important: chronological age alone is an inadequate measure of cardiovascular vulnerability, treatment tolerance, and recovery potential. Clinical assessment should increasingly consider biological age—the cumulative physiological and functional consequences of health and disease across the life course [1-3]. The Central Illustration, “Impact of Health Trajectory on Biologic Age,” provides a useful framework for translating geroscience into cardiovascular practice. Two individuals of the same chronological age may have markedly different biological ages because of differences in lifelong exposure to hypertension, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, poor diet, inflammation, vascular injury, and other adverse health determinants [2-5]. Biological aging therefore reflects more than the passage of time; it represents the progressive accumulation of molecular, cellular, physiological, and functional changes that influence resilience and vulnerability [2,3]. From a cardiovascular perspective, successful prevention should consequently extend beyond avoiding myocardial infarction or stroke to preserving cognition, mobility, muscle strength, independence, and functional capacity. Cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline, and frailty share several important upstream determinants, including hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, obesity, smoking, sedentary behavior, poor dietary quality, vascular dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and loss of skeletal-muscle reserve [3-6]. Frailty is particularly relevant because it reflects declining physiological resilience and can substantially modify the risks and benefits of cardiovascular interventions [1,7,8]. Similarly, cognitive impairment may influence medication adherence, informed decision-making, rehabilitation participation, and post-discharge recovery [1]. Cardiovascular care in older adults must therefore move beyond a disease-centered model toward a function-centered approach in which survival, cognition, mobility, independence, and quality of life are considered alongside conventional cardiovascular outcomes [1,6-8]. Why This Matters for Pakistan The biological-aging framework assumes particular importance in Pakistan because cardiometabolic risk factors frequently emerge long before patients enter specialist cardiovascular care. The Pakistan STEPS survey demonstrated a substantial burden of modifiable risk factors: 96.5% of adults consumed fewer than five servings of fruits and vegetables per day, 41.5% had low physical activity, 26.3% were overweight, 14.9% were obese, while stage I and stage II hypertension affected 37% and 15.9%, respectively [9]. These findings indicate that adverse cardiovascular and biological-aging trajectories may begin decades before overt cardiovascular disease becomes clinically apparent. Pakistan is also experiencing a rapid nutrition and lifestyle transition. Traditional dietary patterns increasingly coexist with greater consumption of commercially prepared and energy-dense foods, refined carbohydrates, fats, salt, and added sugars, particularly in urban populations [10]. This transition is occurring alongside reduced habitual physical activity and changing occupational and urban lifestyles. Such exposures are not merely conventional cardiovascular risk factors; accumulated over decades, they may contribute to vascular injury, metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, loss of physiological reserve, and ultimately accelerated biological aging [2-5]. This is where Pakistan differs importantly from many high-income healthcare settings. While geriatric cardiology increasingly incorporates frailty assessment, rehabilitation, cognitive evaluation, exercise, and shared decision-making, Pakistan must simultaneously address more fundamental barriers to healthy aging. These include delayed detection of hypertension and diabetes, fragmented preventive care, out-of-pocket healthcare expenditure, limited availability of cardiac rehabilitation, and minimal routine assessment of cognition and frailty. Consequently, cardiovascular disease may become clinically evident only after considerable physiological and functional reserve has already been lost. From Cardiovascular Prevention to Preservation of Biological Reserve The implications for prevention are substantial. Blood-pressure control, diabetes prevention, smoking cessation, regular physical activity, healthier dietary patterns, and maintenance of healthy body weight should not be viewed solely as strategies for reducing myocardial infarction and stroke. They should also be understood as interventions that may help preserve vascular, cognitive, metabolic, and functional reserve across the life course [4,5,11]. The INTERHEART study demonstrated the major contribution of modifiable risk factors to myocardial infarction across diverse populations [4], while the PURE study reinforced the importance of modifiable metabolic and behavioral factors for cardiovascular disease and mortality across countries at different income levels [5]. These findings are highly relevant to Pakistan: preventing cardiovascular disease earlier in life may also contribute to healthier aging later in life. For clinicians, implementation of this concept does not require sophisticated biomarkers or expensive biological-age testing. A practical approach could begin with brief assessment of frailty, cognition, mobility, nutrition, medication burden, and social support alongside conventional cardiovascular evaluation [1,7,8]. Simple measures such as gait speed, chair-rise performance, or validated frailty scales may provide clinically meaningful information about physiological reserve. Older adults admitted with acute coronary syndrome, heart failure, valvular heart disease, or arrhythmias should therefore be assessed not only according to ejection fraction, angiographic anatomy, and traditional risk scores, but also according to whether they can walk independently, understand and adhere to treatment, tolerate rehabilitation, manage polypharmacy, and recover function after discharge [1,7,8]. These dimensions may profoundly influence whether technically successful cardiovascular treatment translates into meaningful patient-centered recovery. The same principle extends beyond hospitals. Population-level interventions addressing hypertension, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, obesity, and other major modifiable risk factors can influence the health trajectory long before biological reserve is depleted [11]. In a country with a large population exposed to cardiometabolic risks, preservation of healthy aging should therefore become part of cardiovascular prevention rather than being considered exclusively a geriatric concern. A Broader Definition of Cardiovascular Success The major contribution of the ACC Scientific Statement is its ability to connect cardiology with geroscience, cognition, frailty, and functional health [1]. It challenges cardiovascular medicine to look beyond procedural success and short-term event reduction toward outcomes that matter deeply to older adults: preserved cognition, mobility, independence, functional recovery, and quality of life. For Pakistan, this perspective has particular urgency. If health trajectories influence biological age, then hypertension, diabetes, poor diet, physical inactivity, rapid lifestyle transition, and gaps in preventive healthcare are not simply background public-health problems; they are determinants of how rapidly cardiovascular and functional reserve may decline. The next decade of cardiovascular prevention in Pakistan should therefore broaden its objective from preventing cardiovascular events to preserving biological and functional reserve across the life course. This requires earlier risk-factor detection, stronger primary prevention, greater access to rehabilitation, and routine consideration of frailty and cognition in older cardiovascular patients. Ultimately, the success of cardiovascular care should be judged not only by how many years are added to life, but also by how much cognitive, physical, and functional health is preserved within those years. title: Reliability Testing of the CollaboRATE and SHARED Patient-Reported Measures of Shared Decision Making within Surgical Treatment Pathways: A Mixed-Methods Study
authors: Vignesh Gopalan; Christin Hoffmann; Hilary Bekker; Samuel Lawday; Andrew Judge; Della Hopkins; Jane M. Blazeby; KERRY N. L. AVERY; Angus McNair
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives To evaluate the test-retest reliability of two instruments measuring shared decision-making (SDM) and to explore factors affecting the stability of participant’s lived experience of SDM during the test-retest interval. Design Mixed-methods prospective cohort study, nested within an ongoing National Health Service (NHS, United Kingdom) Trust Quality Improvement study Setting Seven surgical specialties within a tertiary NHS Hospital Trust. Participants/Procedures Patients (>18 years) booked for elective surgical interventions were invited to complete two measurement instruments at each timepoint: CollaboRATE (a 3-item questionnaire developed to assess patients’ perception of professionals SDM skills) and SHARED (a 10-item questionnaire to assess patients’ experience of making a treatment decision with health professionals). Instruments were completed at baseline timepoint (date of surgery booking consultation) and 5-10 days after consultation, but prior to surgery (retest timepoint). Main outcome measures Intra-class correlation (two-way, mixed, absolute agreement) and Kappa coefficients at item, total- and top-score levels were calculated. Bland-Altman plots were used to describe agreement between initial and retest measurement for each instrument. Semi-structured interviews to explore participants’ lived experience were conducted remotely after retest measurement with a purposively selected sample of patients of varying socio-demographic characteristics, surgical specialties, and direction of score change. Transcriptions underwent thematic analysis using inductive coding approaches to identify themes. Results 86 patients completed retest measurements (median time to completion = 8 days). Test-retest reliability was weak for CollaboRATE (ICC=0.34, p<0.001) and moderate for SHARED (ICC=0.52, p<0.001) total scores. Test-retest reliability was moderate for CollaboRATE top score (κ = 0.47, p<0.001). Interviews with nine patients identified two key themes driving instability in the test-retest interval: 1) ongoing reflection on the SDM process, and 2) a need for more support for SDM. Conclusion Our study demonstrated weak-moderate reliability in measuring patient-reported SDM which may be explained by patients’ continued reflection on decisions after surgical consultations. Future research should consider the fact that SDM is a process, and work is needed to understand how and when to optimally measure SDM so that the impact of continued reflection and reasoning are not missed. KEY MESSAGES What is already known on this topic? Instruments (e.g. self-reported questionnaires) measuring SDM from the patient perspective are widely used in clinical pathways, in research, and to guide the development of healthcare services. Few studies have evaluated the test-retest reliability of these instruments, and those done to date report poor reliability. What this study adds? This mixed-methods study explored the test-retest reliability of two SDM measurement instruments in the context of decision-making around surgical interventions. It is the first to supplement standard test-retest methods with interviews to explore patients’ perceptions of SDM over time in this setting. We found that patients reflect on decision-making processes and consider how this may affect the interpretation of reliability metrics in the context of SDM measurement. Our results affirm the dynamic nature of SDM and suggest that test-retest reliability may therefore not be an indicator of the overall quality of an SDM measure when used in this context. How this study might affect research, practice or policy – summarise the implications of this study SDM measurement instruments have different levels of reliability. Routine SDM measurement may identify a subgroup of patients who reflectively question their decisions for medical treatment in the time following consultation. There is scope to target interventions to improve SDM in the period between consultation and procedure. Clinicians and policymakers should design pathways with the timing of SDM measurement kept in mind.
